proofs.proof_tex:
Write \(E_c=\vec E\cap(c\times c)\).  First suppose that the edge witnesses exist.  By \texttt{ass:bias-box}, \(b_i\in[\nu_i^-,\nu_i^+]\) for every \(i\).  By \texttt{ass:positive-ratio}, for every \((j,k)\in E_c\),
\[
 b_j=r_{jk}b_k,\qquad 0<\ell_{jk}\le r_{jk}\le u_{jk}.
\]
Thus \(b_k=0\) if and only if \(b_j=0\), and, if they are nonzero, \(\operatorname{sgn}(b_j)=\operatorname{sgn}(b_k)\).  Connectivity propagates both conclusions along every undirected path in \(c\).  Hence either \(b_c=0\), or all coordinates of \(b_c\) are nonzero and have a common sign.  In the positive case multiplication of \(\ell_{jk}\le r_{jk}\le u_{jk}\) by \(b_k>0\) gives
\[
 \ell_{jk}b_k\le b_j\le u_{jk}b_k,
\]
so \(b_c\in\mathcal P_c^+\) by \texttt{def:positive-branch}.  In the negative case multiplication by \(b_k<0\) reverses the inequalities and gives
\[
 u_{jk}b_k\le b_j\le\ell_{jk}b_k,
\]
so \(b_c\in\mathcal P_c^-\) by \texttt{def:negative-branch}.  The all-zero vector belongs to either branch precisely when the componentwise boxes contain zero.  Applying this argument independently to all components and using \texttt{def:sharp-bias-set} yields \(b\in\mathcal B_G\).

Conversely, suppose \(b\in\mathcal B_G\).  Fix \(c\).  If \(b_c\in\mathcal P_c^+\), the edge inequalities and \(\ell_{jk}>0\) imply that a zero at either endpoint of an edge forces a zero at the other endpoint.  Thus connectivity implies either \(b_c=0\), or \(b_i>0\) for every \(i\in c\).  In the latter case define
\[
 r_{jk}=\frac{b_j}{b_k}\quad((j,k)\in E_c).
\]
Division is valid because \(b_k>0\), and the defining inequalities for \(\mathcal P_c^+\) give \(r_{jk}\in[\ell_{jk},u_{jk}]\).  If \(b_c=0\), choose any \(r_{jk}\in[\ell_{jk},u_{jk}]\), which is possible because the interval is nonempty by \texttt{ass:positive-ratio}.  The proof for \(b_c\in\mathcal P_c^-\) is identical after noting that division by \(b_k<0\) reverses both displayed inequalities.  The witnesses can be chosen component by component because no edge joins distinct components.  This proves both directions, including the closure point \(b_c=0\).

Fix \(B\in\mathcal B_G\), and write \(\tau_i^2=\operatorname{Var}_{P_{\mathrm{obs}}}(U_i)\).  Positive definiteness in \texttt{ass:gaussian-observed-submodel} gives \(\tau_i^2>0\).  The construction in \texttt{def:gaussian-completion} augments one unchanged draw from \(P_{\mathrm{obs}}\); consequently its observed margin, including every cross-setting covariance of \((X,D,Y)\), is exactly \(P_{\mathrm{obs}}\).  The construction changes no observed coordinate.

If \(B_i\ne0\), then \(A_i^B=D_i+U_i/B_i\), \(f_i^B(A_i^B)=B_iA_i^B\), and \(\varepsilon_i^B=0\).  Therefore
\[
 (s_i-B_i)D_i+B_i\left(D_i+\frac{U_i}{B_i}\right)
 =s_iD_i+U_i=Y_i.
\]
Conditional mean independence of the zero disturbance is immediate.  Conditional on \(X\), the pair \((D_i,U_i)\) is jointly Gaussian, has variances \(1\) and \(\tau_i^2\), and has covariance zero.  The Gaussian conditional-variance formula, obtained directly by taking the Schur complement of
\[
 \operatorname{Var}(D_i,A_i^B\mid X)
 =\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&1+\tau_i^2/B_i^2\end{pmatrix},
\]
therefore gives
\[
 \operatorname{Var}(D_i\mid X,A_i^B)
 =1-\frac{1}{1+\tau_i^2/B_i^2}
 =\frac{\tau_i^2}{B_i^2+\tau_i^2}>0.
\]
The conditional law does not depend on \(X\), as required by the observed-submodel assumption.

If \(B_i=0\), then \(A_i^B=Z_i\), \(f_i^B=0\), \(\varepsilon_i^B=U_i\), and again
\[
 (s_i-B_i)D_i+\varepsilon_i^B=s_iD_i+U_i=Y_i.
\]
Residualization gives zero conditional means for \(D_i\) and \(U_i\) given \(X\).  Joint Gaussianity and \(\operatorname{Cov}(D_i,U_i)=0\) imply conditional independence of \(D_i\) and \(U_i\); independence of \(Z\) from the entire observed vector then yields
\[
 E[U_i\mid D_i,X,Z_i]=0,
 \qquad
 \operatorname{Var}(D_i\mid X,Z_i)=1>0.
\]
Thus \texttt{ass:partially-linear-model} holds in both cases.

The long coefficient in the constructed equation is \(\theta_i(P^B)=s_i-B_i\).  Since the observed short coefficient remains \(s_i\), \texttt{def:gaussian-completion} and the definition \(B(P)=s-\theta(P)\) give
\[
 B_i(P^B)=s_i-\theta_i(P^B)=B_i.
\]
The component-sign lemma supplies ratio witnesses for \(B\), while membership of \(B\) in \(\mathcal B_G\) supplies the bias boxes.  Hence \texttt{ass:bias-box} and \texttt{ass:positive-ratio} hold.  Observational equivalence was proved in the first paragraph, and the Gaussian observed-submodel property is a property of the unchanged observed margin.  The member-property definitions \texttt{def:gaussian-completion-class} and \texttt{def:hk-model-class} now imply
\[
 P^B\in\mathcal M_G(P_{\mathrm{obs}})
 \subseteq\mathcal M_{\mathrm{HK}}(P_{\mathrm{obs}}),
 \qquad
 \theta(P^B)=s-B.
\]

Take \(P\in\mathcal M_{\mathrm{HK}}(P_{\mathrm{obs}})\).  Its member properties in \texttt{def:hk-model-class} imply the bias box and positive-ratio restrictions.  By \texttt{lem:component-sign-decomposition}, \(B(P)\in\mathcal B_G\).  Since \(B(P)=s-\theta(P)\),
\[
 \theta(P)=s-B(P)\in s-\mathcal B_G.
\]
Taking all compatible \(P\) in \texttt{def:identified-set} proves
\[
 \Theta_I(P_{\mathrm{obs}})\subseteq s-\mathcal B_G.
\]

For the second containment, fix \(b\in\mathcal B_G\) and set \(\vartheta=s-b\).  The box constraints give
\[
 s_i-\nu_i^+\le\vartheta_i\le s_i-\nu_i^-.
\]
For an edge \((j,k)\), the component-sign lemma supplies \(r\in[\ell_{jk},u_{jk}]\) with \(b_j=rb_k\).  Therefore
\[
 b_j-b_k=(r-1)b_k.
\]
The bilinear function \((r,v)\mapsto(r-1)v\) attains its minimum and maximum on the rectangle \([\ell_{jk},u_{jk}]\times[\nu_k^-,\nu_k^+]\) at a corner: for fixed \(r\) it is affine in \(v\), and after optimizing over the two endpoints in \(v\), each resulting function is affine in \(r\).  Thus, with the quantities in \texttt{def:hk-outer-polytope},
\[
 c_{jk}^-\le b_j-b_k\le c_{jk}^+.
\]
Since \(\vartheta_j-\vartheta_k=(s_j-s_k)-(b_j-b_k)\), every defining inequality of \(\mathcal J_{\mathrm{HK}}\) holds.  Hence \(s-\mathcal B_G\subseteq\mathcal J_{\mathrm{HK}}\).

Now impose \texttt{ass:gaussian-observed-submodel}.  For every \(b\in\mathcal B_G\), \texttt{prop:gaussian-completion-membership} constructs a law \(P^b\in\mathcal M_{\mathrm{HK}}(P_{\mathrm{obs}})\) with \(\theta(P^b)=s-b\).  Consequently \(s-\mathcal B_G\subseteq\Theta_I(P_{\mathrm{obs}})\).  Combining this reverse inclusion with the first one gives equality.  Because the augmentation retains the entire observed draw, this attainability argument imposes no restriction on cross-setting covariances beyond the positive definiteness already stated in the Gaussian observed-submodel assumption.

Fix a component \(c\), a sign \(\zeta\), and first exclude the all-zero vector.  Positive edge ratios and connectivity then imply \(|b_i|>0\) for all \(i\in c\), so the change of variables \(x_i=\log|b_i|\) is well defined and bijective between the nonzero sign stratum and its log magnitudes.  Each ratio inequality is equivalent, by monotonicity of the logarithm, to
\[
 x_j-x_k\le\log u_{jk},\qquad
 x_k-x_j\le-\log\ell_{jk}.
\]
For precision about box boundaries, the positive branch uses the magnitude set
\[
 I_i^+=(0,\infty)\cap[\nu_i^-,\nu_i^+],
\]
and the negative branch uses \(I_i^-=\{-v:v\in(-\infty,0)\cap[\nu_i^-,\nu_i^+]\}\).  If one of these sets is empty, record the elementary inconsistent constraint \(x_i-x_i\le-1\), which is a negative self-cycle.  Otherwise its logarithmic image is an interval; each finite endpoint of that interval gives an upper or lower difference constraint relative to an anchor vertex \(0\) with \(x_0=0\), while an endpoint at \(-\infty\) contributes no finite constraint.  This makes explicit the sign-adjusted box convention in \texttt{def:log-difference-system}.  The resulting system has the form
\[
 x_v-x_u\le w_{uv}\qquad ((u,v)\in E^{\zeta}_{\mathrm{aug}}).
\]

If these inequalities are feasible, summing them around any directed cycle gives \(0\le\sum w_{uv}\), so a negative-weight directed cycle is impossible.  Conversely, adjoin a new super-source, distinct from the anchor used for box bounds, with a zero-weight arc to every old vertex and no incoming arc.  This creates no directed cycle.  Let \(d(v)\) be the minimum weight of a directed walk from the super-source to \(v\).  A minimum exists because any repeated-vertex segment is a nonnegative cycle and can be removed, leaving one of finitely many simple walks.  Appending the arc \((u,v)\) to a shortest walk to \(u\) gives
\[
 d(v)\le d(u)+w_{uv}.
\]
Hence \(x_v=d(v)-d(0)\), where \(0\) is the original anchor, satisfies every difference constraint and has \(x_0=0\).  This proves the negative-cycle alternative without an external theorem.

Let \(A x\le b\) be the same system, with each row of \(A\) equal to the incidence vector \(e_v-e_u\).  A nonnegative vector \(y\) satisfying \(y^\top A=0\) is a nonnegative circulation on the augmented directed graph.  If a negative cycle exists, its arc-incidence vector is such a \(y\) and has \(y^\top b<0\).  Conversely, any nonzero nonnegative circulation has a positive-flow directed cycle: follow positive-flow arcs until a vertex repeats, subtract the minimum flow on that cycle, and iterate.  Finiteness makes the algorithm terminate and represents \(y\) as a nonnegative sum of directed-cycle incidence vectors.  If \(y^\top b<0\), at least one cycle in that sum has negative weight.  Therefore
\[
 \mathcal D_c^{\zeta}\text{ is feasible}
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 \text{there is no negative directed cycle}
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 \nexists y\ge0:\ y^\top A=0,\ y^\top b<0.
\]
Exponentiation recovers exactly the nonzero part of \(\mathcal P_c^{\zeta}\).  The omitted closure point is exactly \(b_c=0\); by the bias boxes it is feasible if and only if \(0\in[\nu_i^-,\nu_i^+]\) for all \(i\in c\).  Positive edge bounds rule out every partially zero vector in a connected component.  The nonzero log test plus this separate zero test is therefore closure-complete.

For computation, fix a sign map \(\zeta:\mathcal C_G\to\{+,-\}\).  Its branch feasible set with pins is
\[
 F_{\zeta}(H,t)=\{b:\ b_c\in\mathcal P_c^{\zeta(c)}\ \forall c,\ H(s-b)=t\}.
\]
By \texttt{def:sharp-bias-set} and \texttt{def:pinned-sharp-set},
\[
 \Theta_I(H,t)=\bigcup_{\zeta}\{s-b:b\in F_{\zeta}(H,t)\}.
\]
There are only \(2^{|\mathcal C_G|}\) branches.  Each \(F_{\zeta}(H,t)\) is a closed subset of the bounded bias box, hence compact.  A linear objective therefore attains its extrema on every nonempty branch, and taking the extrema over this finite union proves exactness of exhaustive branch linear programming, including equality cycles and ties.

It remains to verify the mixed-integer formulation.  If \(z_c=1\), its sign constraints give \(0\le b_i\le M_i\) and the first edge pair reduces to
\[
 \ell_{jk}b_k\le b_j\le u_{jk}b_k.
\]
The second pair is redundant because
\[
 u_{jk}b_k-b_j\le u_{jk}M_k\le M_{jk},
 \qquad
 b_j-\ell_{jk}b_k\le M_j\le M_{jk}.
\]
If \(z_c=0\), the sign constraints give \(-M_i\le b_i\le0\), the second edge pair reduces to
\[
 u_{jk}b_k\le b_j\le\ell_{jk}b_k,
\]
and the first is redundant because
\[
 \ell_{jk}b_k-b_j\le M_j\le M_{jk},
 \qquad
 b_j-u_{jk}b_k\le u_{jk}M_k\le M_{jk}.
\]
All inequalities used only \(M_{jk}=(1+u_{jk})\max\{M_j,M_k\}\) and positivity of \(u_{jk}\) and \(\ell_{jk}\).  Conversely, every point of either branch satisfies the corresponding active inequalities and the just-verified redundant ones.  Hence the MILP bias projection is exactly \(\mathcal B_G\), and adding the same pin equality and objective gives the same attained extrema as branch enumeration.

If \(M_i=0\), its box is the singleton \(b_i=0\).  On either active sign branch, an incident ratio edge and \(\ell_{jk}>0\) force the other endpoint to zero; connectivity iterates this implication through the component.  In the stated two-vertex check, \(M_1=0\), \(M_2=1\), and
\[
 M_{12}=(1+2)\max\{0,1\}=3.
\]
The first coordinate is zero and the active edge forces the second coordinate to zero on either sign branch.  Thus both exact formulations project to \(\{(0,0)\}\), as claimed.

In this two-setting family there is one connected component.  The two branch definitions inside \texttt{def:sharp-bias-set} imply directly that every nonzero feasible bias has a common sign and satisfies \(b_1/b_2\in[1/R,R]\).  Symmetry of the bias set implies
\[
 \min_{b\in\mathcal B_G}(b_1-b_2)
 =-\max_{b\in\mathcal B_G}(b_1-b_2).
\]
On the nonnegative branch, for fixed \(b_1\), the smallest feasible \(b_2\) is \(b_1/R\); hence
\[
 \max_{b\in\mathcal P^+}(b_1-b_2)
 =\max_{0\le b_1\le a}b_1(1-R^{-1})
 =a(1-R^{-1}).
\]
The negative branch has the same maximum after interchanging magnitudes.  Therefore
\[
 h_{s-\mathcal B_G}(q_{12})
 =(s_1-s_2)+a(1-R^{-1}).
\]

For \(\mathcal J_{\mathrm{HK}}\), the coordinate boxes alone allow the effect difference to deviate from \(s_1-s_2\) by at most \(2a\).  The four-corner calculation in \texttt{def:hk-outer-polytope} gives
\[
 c_{12}^-=-a(R-1),\qquad c_{12}^+=a(R-1),
\]
because \(R-1>1-R^{-1}>0\).  Intersecting the coordinate and difference restrictions yields
\[
 h_{\mathcal J_{\mathrm{HK}}}(q_{12})
 =(s_1-s_2)+a\min\{2,R-1\}.
\]
Subtracting the two displays gives the asserted formula.  It is strictly positive: if \(1<R\le3\),
\[
 (R-1)-(1-R^{-1})=\frac{(R-1)^2}{R}>0,
\]
whereas if \(R\ge3\),
\[
 2-(1-R^{-1})=1+R^{-1}>0.
\]
A strict support-function inequality implies strict set containment, while \texttt{thm:sharp-sign-ratio-closure} supplies the non-strict containment.

For a sign map \(\zeta\), let
\[
 F^0_{\zeta}=\{b:b_c\in\mathcal P_c^{\zeta(c)}\ \forall c\},
 \qquad
 F_{\zeta}(H,t)=F^0_{\zeta}\cap\{b:H(s-b)=t\}.
\]
The finite-union identity established in \texttt{thm:cycle-farkas-and-computation} gives
\[
 \Theta_I(H,t)=\bigcup_{\zeta}\{s-b:b\in F_{\zeta}(H,t)\}.
\]
Consequently the lower and upper supports in direction \(q\) are exactly the minimum and maximum of \(q^\top(s-b)\) over the feasible branch linear programs.

For completeness, the advertised classification is finite and certifiable.  Put every branch inequality in the form \(G_\zeta b\le g_\zeta\).  We first derive the needed finite-dimensional alternative.  For a generic system \(Gb\le g\), \(Hb=h\), form the polyhedral cone
\[
 \mathcal K=\{(Gb+r,Hb):b\in\mathbb R^K,\ r\in[0,\infty)^m\}.
\]
It is the sum of a finite-dimensional subspace and a cone generated by the finitely many coordinate rays; after quotienting by the subspace it is finitely generated and hence closed.  The system is feasible exactly when \((g,h)\in\mathcal K\).  If it is infeasible, take the Euclidean projection of \((g,h)\) onto the closed convex cone \(\mathcal K\).  The projection inequality supplies a separating vector \((y,\lambda)\) that is nonnegative on \(\mathcal K\) and negative at \((g,h)\).  Varying \(b\) through both signs and \(r\) through the nonnegative coordinate rays forces
\[
 y^\top G+\lambda^\top H=0,\qquad y\ge0,\qquad
 y^\top g+\lambda^\top h<0.
\]
Conversely, these three relations contradict feasibility after multiplication of the primal inequalities by \(y\).  This proves the alternative.

Apply it with \(h=Hs-t\).  Feasibility of the pins is a phase-I linear program; if infeasible, replacing \(\lambda\) by \(-\lambda\) supplies multipliers \(y\ge0\) and \(\lambda\) such that
\[
 y^\top G_\zeta-\lambda^\top H=0,
 \qquad
 y^\top g_\zeta+\lambda^\top(t-Hs)<0,
\]
which is a directly checkable primal--dual infeasibility certificate.  If feasible, the pin system is redundant exactly when, for every row \(h_r^\top\) of \(H\), both branch linear programs
\[
 \min_{b\in F^0_\zeta}\{h_r^\top(s-b)-t_r\},
 \qquad
 \max_{b\in F^0_\zeta}\{h_r^\top(s-b)-t_r\}
\]
have value zero.  Otherwise the nonempty slice is a proper face or section and the pin system is jointly binding.  Thus infeasible, redundant, and feasible-proper are exhaustive, and every decision is accompanied by primal optimizers or the displayed dual certificate.

Now set \(R=2\) in the symmetric two-setting family and impose \(\theta_1=s_1-a\), equivalently \(b_1=a\).  A negative branch is impossible, and the positive ratio restriction gives
\[
 \frac12\le\frac{b_1}{b_2}\le2,\qquad 0\le b_2\le a.
\]
Since \(b_1=a\), this is equivalent to \(a/2\le b_2\le a\).  Therefore
\[
 \theta_2=s_2-b_2\in[s_2-a,s_2-a/2].
\]
For the outer polytope, the coordinate restriction is \(\theta_2\in[s_2-a,s_2+a]\), and its difference restriction is
\[
 (s_1-s_2)-a\le\theta_1-\theta_2\le(s_1-s_2)+a.
\]
Substitution of \(\theta_1=s_1-a\) and intersection with the coordinate interval gives \(\theta_2\in[s_2-a,s_2]\).  The upper endpoints differ by \(a/2\).

The equality edge \((3,1)\) has \(\ell_{31}=u_{31}=1\), so every feasible vector satisfies \(b_3=b_1\).  Write \(x=b_1=b_3\) and \(y=b_2\).  On the nonnegative branch, either both are zero or the edges \((1,2)\) and \((2,3)\) give the same pair of inequalities
\[
 \frac{x}{2}\le y\le2x.
\]
Intersecting with \(0\le x,y\le a\) gives
\[
 0\le x\le a,\qquad \frac{x}{2}\le y\le\min\{2x,a\}.
\]
On the nonpositive branch, division is unnecessary: the defining reversed inequalities give
\[
 2x\le y\le\frac{x}{2}.
\]
Intersecting with \(-a\le x,y\le0\) gives
\[
 -a\le x\le0,\qquad \max\{2x,-a\}\le y\le\frac{x}{2}.
\]
Their only zero-stratum point is \((0,0,0)\), because any zero propagates around the connected cycle by positivity of all ratio lower bounds.  These calculations prove the displayed formula for \(\mathcal B_G\).

On a nonzero branch, put \(w_i=\log|b_i|\).  The equality edge contributes
\[
 w_3-w_1\le0,\qquad w_1-w_3\le0,
\]
and therefore forces \(w_1=w_3\).  Its two arcs form a zero-weight directed cycle.  Every other ratio arc has weight \(\log2\ge0\), so every remaining directed cycle has nonnegative total weight.  This is consistent with, and certifies, the nonempty log branch by \texttt{thm:cycle-farkas-and-computation}.

The pins \(H_3\theta=t_3\) are equivalent to \(b_1=b_3=a\).  Hence only the positive branch survives and the preceding formula gives \(a/2\le b_2\le a\).  Thus the sharp slice is
\[
 \{(s_1-a,\theta_2,s_3-a):\theta_2\in[s_2-a,s_2-a/2]\}.
\]
For the outer set, the equality edge enforces the already satisfied relation between the first and third pinned effects.  Each of the two remaining edge-difference restrictions, after substitution of the corresponding pin, permits \(\theta_2\in[s_2-2a,s_2]\); intersection with its coordinate box \([s_2-a,s_2+a]\) gives \([s_2-a,s_2]\).  The upper-endpoint gap is therefore \(a/2\).

Write \(d_j=d_j(\mu)\) and \(d_k=d_k(\mu)\).  If \(d_jd_k>0\) and \(b_jb_k>0\), division by the positive number \(b_k^2d_jd_k\) gives
\[
 \frac{Q_{jk}(b,\mu)}{b_k^2d_jd_k}
 =\left(\frac{b_j}{b_k}-\frac{d_j}{d_k}\right)
  \left(\frac{b_j}{b_k}-\frac{d_k}{d_j}\right).
\]
The product of two real linear factors is nonpositive exactly between its two roots.  This proves the reciprocal-ratio assertion.  If \(b_j=b_k=0\), then \(Q_{jk}=0\).  If exactly one bias coordinate is zero while the other is not, then \(Q_{jk}=b_m^2d_jd_k>0\) for the nonzero bias coordinate \(m\); hence there are no omitted cases under \(b_jb_k\ge0\).

If \(d_k=0\) and \(d_j\ne0\), direct multiplication gives
\[
 Q_{jk}=(-b_kd_j)(b_jd_j)=-b_jb_kd_j^2\le0.
\]
If \(d_j=0\) and \(d_k\ne0\), it gives \(Q_{jk}=-b_jb_kd_k^2\le0\).  Both inequalities use the stated branch condition \(b_jb_k\ge0\).  Finally, if \(d_j=d_k=0\), both factors in the definition of \(Q_{jk}\) vanish.  These identities cover every zero-denominator case without division.

Let \(X_{nr}=h(O_{nr})-\mu_n\) and \(\bar X_n=n^{-1}\sum_rX_{nr}\).  Then
\[
 \widehat\Omega_n=\frac1n\sum_{r=1}^nX_{nr}X_{nr}^\top-\bar X_n\bar X_n^\top.
\]
Because \(p\) is fixed and \(E\|X_{n1}\|^{4+\delta}\le C\), row-wise independence gives, uniformly over admissible arrays,
\[
 E\left\|\frac1n\sum_{r=1}^n
   \{X_{nr}X_{nr}^\top-\Omega_n\}\right\|_F^2
 \le \frac1n E\|X_{n1}X_{n1}^\top-\Omega_n\|_F^2
 \le\frac{C_1}{n},
\]
and
\[
 E\|\bar X_n\|^2=\frac{\operatorname{tr}(\Omega_n)}n\le\frac{pC}{n}.
\]
Markov's inequality and \(\|A\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le\|A\|_F\) therefore imply
\[
 \sup_{(P_n)}P_n\{\|\widehat\Omega_n-\Omega_n\|_{\mathrm{op}}>\varepsilon\}\longrightarrow0.
\]
Since \(\widehat\Omega_n\) is positive semidefinite and \(\lambda_n>0\), \(\widetilde\Omega_n=\widehat\Omega_n+\lambda_nI_p\) is positive definite on every sample.

Put \(T_n=n\bar X_n^\top\Omega_n^{-1}\bar X_n\) and \(\widetilde T_n=n\bar X_n^\top\widetilde\Omega_n^{-1}\bar X_n\).  The covariance eigenvalue bound gives \(n\|\bar X_n\|^2=O_P(1)\) uniformly.  On the event \(\|\widetilde\Omega_n-\Omega_n\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le c/2\), the smallest eigenvalue of \(\widetilde\Omega_n\) is at least \(c/2\), and the inverse identity yields
\[
 \|\widetilde\Omega_n^{-1}-\Omega_n^{-1}\|_{\mathrm{op}}
 \le \frac{2}{c^2}\|\widetilde\Omega_n-\Omega_n\|_{\mathrm{op}}.
\]
Covariance consistency and \(\lambda_n\to0\) make the right side \(o_P(1)\) uniformly.  Hence
\[
 |\widetilde T_n-T_n|
 \le n\|\bar X_n\|^2
 \|\widetilde\Omega_n^{-1}-\Omega_n^{-1}\|_{\mathrm{op}}
 =o_P(1)
\]
uniformly, which is the claimed regularized Slutsky equivalence.

The deterministic part is immediate from \texttt{def:inversion-confidence-set}: if \(\mu_n\in\mathcal U_n\), then the term indexed by \(\mu=\mu_n\) occurs in the union, and hence
\[
 \mathcal R_{\mathrm{ss}}(\mu_n)
 \subseteq\bigcup_{\mu\in\mathcal U_n}\mathcal R_{\mathrm{ss}}(\mu)
 =\mathcal C_n^{\mathrm{inv}}.
\]

For probabilistic coverage, set \(X_{nr}=\Omega_n^{-1/2}\{h(O_{nr})-\mu_n\}\).  Then \(E X_{n1}=0\), \(E[X_{n1}X_{n1}^\top]=I_p\), and the moment and eigenvalue assumptions give a uniform bound on \(E\|X_{n1}\|^{3}\).  For fixed \(t\in\mathbb R^p\), Taylor expansion of \(e^{iu}\) with its third-order remainder gives
\[
 E\exp\left\{i\frac{t^\top X_{n1}}{\sqrt n}\right\}
 =1-\frac{\|t\|^2}{2n}+R_n(t),
 \qquad
 |R_n(t)|\le \frac{C_t}{n^{3/2}},
\]
uniformly over the admissible rows.  Raising this expression to the \(n\)-th power and using row-wise independence yields
\[
 E\exp\left\{it^\top n^{-1/2}\sum_{r=1}^nX_{nr}\right\}
 \longrightarrow e^{-\|t\|^2/2}
\]
uniformly.  A contradiction subsequence argument together with the characteristic-function continuity theorem therefore gives the uniform fixed-dimensional central limit conclusion
\[
 \sqrt n\,\Omega_n^{-1/2}(\bar h_n-\mu_n)\Rightarrow N(0,I_p).
\]
The squared Euclidean norm consequently converges uniformly to \(\chi_p^2\).  By \texttt{lem:regularized-covariance-slutsky} and continuity of the \(\chi_p^2\) distribution at its \((1-\alpha)\)-quantile,
\[
 \inf_{(P_n)}P_n\{\mu_n\in\mathcal U_n\}
 =\inf_{(P_n)}P_n\!\left\{
 n(\bar h_n-\mu_n)^\top\widetilde\Omega_n^{-1}(\bar h_n-\mu_n)
 \le\chi^2_{p,1-\alpha}\right\}
 \longrightarrow1-\alpha.
\]
Combining this with the deterministic event inclusion proves the asserted lower coverage bound.  No step divided by a coordinate of \(d(\mu_n)\), selected a component sign, or selected an optimizer basis.  The argument is therefore unchanged at exact zeros, root-\(n\) weak coordinates, and all indicated ties.

The nonzero conditions on \(d_i(\mu_0)\) and on \(d_j(\mu_0)^2-d_k(\mu_0)^2\) persist on a neighborhood by continuity of \(\Gamma\).  On that neighborhood \texttt{lem:undivided-supershort-equivalence} converts every quadratic edge restriction into one of two linear ratio inequalities, with the ordering of the reciprocal ratios fixed.  The coefficients of those inequalities are continuously differentiable functions of \(\mu\), since every denominator is bounded away from zero there.

Strictly positive branch-selection margins keep the same component-sign branch uniquely optimal.  Strict primal and dual slacks and strictly positive reduced-cost margins keep the same unique primal--dual basis: by continuity, the basic solution remains feasible, the nonbasic reduced costs retain their signs, and every competing branch remains separated in objective value.  On this neighborhood each endpoint is therefore the value of one fixed finite-dimensional linear-program basis.  Solving the active equalities gives a continuously differentiable rational expression in the constraint coefficients, because the basis matrix remains nonsingular.  Composition with the continuously differentiable map \(\Gamma\) proves that \(\psi_q\) is continuously differentiable there, with derivative \(J_q\).

For the fixed law, put \(X_r=\Omega_0^{-1/2}\{h(O_r)-\mu_0\}\).  The sampling and moment assumptions give \(E X_r=0\), \(E[X_rX_r^\top]=I_p\), and \(E\|X_r\|^3<\infty\).  For every fixed \(t\), the third-order expansion
\[
 E e^{it^\top X_r/\sqrt n}
 =1-\frac{\|t\|^2}{2n}+O(n^{-3/2})
\]
and independence show that the characteristic function of \(n^{-1/2}\sum_rX_r\) converges to \(e^{-\|t\|^2/2}\).  Thus
\[
 \sqrt n(\bar h_n-\mu_0)\Rightarrow N(0,\Omega_0).
\]
Differentiability yields the expansion
\[
 \psi_q(\bar h_n)-\psi_q(\mu_0)
 =J_q(\mu_0)(\bar h_n-\mu_0)+r_n,
 \qquad
 \frac{\|r_n\|}{\|\bar h_n-\mu_0\|}\to_{P_0}0,
\]
and hence the displayed Gaussian limit.

For column \(m\), the fundamental theorem of calculus on the stable neighborhood gives
\[
 \widehat J_{q,n}^{(m)}
 =\int_0^1J_q(\bar h_n+t\varepsilon_ne_m)e_m\,dt.
\]
Because \(\bar h_n\to_{P_0}\mu_0\) and \(\varepsilon_n\to0\), continuity implies \(\widehat J_{q,n}\to_{P_0}J_q(\mu_0)\).  The extra condition \(\sqrt n\varepsilon_n\to\infty\) is compatible with, but stronger than, what this fixed-cell consistency step needs.  The covariance lemma gives \(\widetilde\Omega_n\to_{P_0}\Omega_0\), so
\[
 \widehat J_{q,n}\widetilde\Omega_n\widehat J_{q,n}^\top
 -J_q(\bar h_n)\widetilde\Omega_nJ_q(\bar h_n)^\top
 \to_{P_0}0.
\]
If the two limiting diagonal variances are positive, continuity of the square root shows that the corresponding standard-error factors differ by \(o_{P_0}(1)\).  The interval centers are identical and their half-widths carry the factor \(n^{-1/2}\); every corresponding endpoint difference is therefore \(o_{P_0}(n^{-1/2})\).  All stability claims are local to the fixed law, so the conclusion is pointwise, not uniform over shrinking margins.

theorem.statement:
Fix \(q\in\mathbb R^K\).  There is an explicit split-sample realization of \(\mathsf H_n\) with the following properties.  Use a pilot of size \(m_n=\lfloor n^{2/3}\rfloor\) and an independent inference subsample of size \(N_n=n-m_n\).  A conservative pilot safe-cell test selects numerical-delta inference only when a shrinking joint neighborhood of the pilot primitive mean and covariance lies inside one cell having nonzero ratio-order, branch-selection, primal-slack, dual-slack, reduced-cost, and endpoint-variance margins; otherwise it selects primitive-moment inversion.  On inversion selection, \(\mathsf H_n\) is the inference-subsample version of \(\mathcal C_n^{\mathrm{inv}}\).  On safe-cell selection, \(\mathsf H_n\) is the slab whose lower and upper \(q\)-support limits are, respectively, the lower endpoint of the first numerical-delta interval and the upper endpoint of the second numerical-delta interval, both computed on the inference subsample.  Then
\[
 \liminf_{n\to\infty}\inf_{(P_n)}P_n\{\mathcal R_{\mathrm{ss}}(\mu_n)\subseteq\mathsf H_n\}\ge1-\alpha.
\]
The pilot selects inversion with probability tending to one uniformly along exact-zero or \(n^{-1/2}\)-weak denominator sequences and along exact or \(n^{-1/2}\)-weak ratio-order, component-branch, or optimizer-basis ties.  At every fixed law \(P_0\) satisfying all strict-cell conditions of \texttt{thm:pointwise-regular-cell-oracle-recovery} and having two positive endpoint variances, the pilot selects the safe cell with probability tending to one, and the two finite \(q\)-support endpoints of \(\mathsf H_n\) differ from the corresponding outer endpoints of \(\mathcal I_{q,n}^{\mathrm{or}}\) by \(o_{P_0}(n^{-1/2})\).
theorem.proof_tex:
We give the thresholds and prove both assertions.  There are finitely many component-sign branches and finitely many primal--dual bases.  Let \(\mathcal G\) be the set of pairs \((\mu,\Omega)\) for which the two endpoint problems lie in one of the strict cells described in \texttt{thm:pointwise-regular-cell-oracle-recovery} and both quantities
\[
 g_r(\mu)^\top\Omega g_r(\mu),\qquad
 g_r(\mu)=D\psi_{q,r}(\mu),\qquad r\in\{1,2\},
\]
are positive.  For integer \(j\ge1\), define \(G_j\) as the finite union, over cells and bases, of the closed subsets on which
\[
 \|\mu\|\le j,\quad j^{-1}I_p\preceq\Omega\preceq jI_p,\quad
 \text{every stated strict-cell margin is at least }j^{-1},\quad
 j^{-1}\le g_r(\mu)^\top\Omega g_r(\mu)\le j,\quad
 \|g_r(\mu)\|\le j.
\]
Empty pieces are discarded.  Each \(G_j\) is compact, the sequence may be made nested by replacing \(G_j\) with \(\bigcup_{k\le j}G_k\), and
\[
 \mathcal G=\bigcup_{j\ge1}G_j.
\]
All margins are computable by the finite branch and basis linear programs of \texttt{thm:cycle-farkas-and-computation}.  On each \(G_j\), let \(\omega_j(r)\) be the maximum oscillation of the two endpoint Jacobian rows between points at distance at most \(r\) that remain in the certified cell.  Compactness and continuity give \(\omega_j(r)\downarrow0\) as \(r\downarrow0\).

Let \(\varepsilon_{N_n}\) be the numerical-difference step on the inference subsample.  Define \(j_n\) to be the largest integer \(j\le m_n^{1/4}\) such that
\[
 \omega_j\left(3j/\sqrt{m_n}+\varepsilon_{N_n}\right)\le j^{-2}
 \quad\text{and}\quad j^3\le\sqrt{m_n};
\]
put \(j_n=1\) if the set is empty.  For every fixed \(j\), both inequalities hold eventually, so a diagonal argument gives
\[
 j_n\to\infty,\qquad j_n/\sqrt{m_n}\to0,\qquad
 j_n\omega_{j_n}(3j_n/\sqrt{m_n}+\varepsilon_{N_n})\to0.
\]
This is an explicit deterministic threshold sequence because the finite cell maps and their moduli are known functions of the primitive moments.

Compute the pilot mean \(\bar h_n^{\mathrm p}\) and covariance \(\widehat\Omega_n^{\mathrm p}\) by the frozen formulas with sample size \(m_n\).  Select the regular procedure if and only if the closed product-norm ball
\[
 \mathbb B\left((\bar h_n^{\mathrm p},\widehat\Omega_n^{\mathrm p}),
                  3j_n/\sqrt{m_n}+\varepsilon_{N_n}\right)
\]
is contained in one component of \(G_{j_n}\).  This condition exposes simultaneous thresholds for the primitive mean, covariance, ratio order, branch gap, primal and dual slack, reduced cost, and endpoint variance.  It can be certified by finite branch/basis enumeration and interval optimization on the displayed ball.

The moment calculations in \texttt{lem:regularized-covariance-slutsky}, applied to the pilot, imply
\[
 \sup_{(P_n)}P_n\left\{
 \|\bar h_n^{\mathrm p}-\mu_n\|+
 \|\widehat\Omega_n^{\mathrm p}-\Omega_n\|_{\mathrm{op}}
 >j_n/\sqrt{m_n}\right\}\longrightarrow0. \tag{1}
\]
Indeed, the mean term follows from Chebyshev's inequality, and the covariance term follows from the fourth-moment calculation there; their tail bounds are \(O(j_n^{-2})\).  On the complement of the event in (1), regular selection implies \((\mu_n,\Omega_n)\in G_{j_n}\).  Conversely, if a zero, order, branch, or basis margin is \(O(n^{-1/2})\), then it is \(o(j_n/\sqrt{m_n})\); the pilot ball intersects the complement of every certified cell with probability tending to one.  Hence inversion is selected uniformly along all sequences listed in the statement.

Use only the independent inference subsample for the selected confidence procedure.  If inversion is selected, apply \texttt{lem:uniform-primitive-inversion} with sample size \(N_n\).  If regular inference is selected and (1) does not occur, the true pair lies in \(G_{j_n}\).  The same characteristic-function expansion used in that lemma is uniform for every standardized linear functional because the covariance eigenvalues are bounded and the third absolute moments are uniformly bounded.  Cell stability and the mean-value formula give, uniformly on \(G_{j_n}\),
\[
 \psi_{q,r}(\bar h_n^{\mathrm i})-\psi_{q,r}(\mu_n)
 =g_r(\mu_n)^\top(\bar h_n^{\mathrm i}-\mu_n)+o_P(N_n^{-1/2}),
\]
where the remainder divided by the linear standard error is bounded in probability by a constant times
\(j_n\omega_{j_n}(3j_n/\sqrt{m_n}+\varepsilon_{N_n})=o(1)\).  The same modulus and the integral finite-difference formula show that the numerical Jacobian consistently estimates \(g_r(\mu_n)\) relative to its standard deviation.  Uniform covariance consistency then studentizes the two rows.  Thus each relevant one-sided normal error probability is at most \(\alpha/2+o(1)\), and the union bound gives
\[
 \inf_{(P_n):(\mu_n,\Omega_n)\in G_{j_n}}
 P_n\left\{
 \underline\psi_q(\mu_n)\ge L_n^{\mathrm{ND}},\ 
 \overline\psi_q(\mu_n)\le U_n^{\mathrm{ND}}
 \right\}\ge1-\alpha-o(1), \tag{2}
\]
where \(L_n^{\mathrm{ND}}\) is the lower outer endpoint for coordinate one and \(U_n^{\mathrm{ND}}\) the upper outer endpoint for coordinate two.

Define the regular output as the slab
\[
 \mathsf H_n^{\mathrm{reg}}=\{\theta\in\mathbb R^K:
 L_n^{\mathrm{ND}}\le q^\top\theta\le U_n^{\mathrm{ND}}\},
\]
and the fallback output as the inference-subsample version of \(\mathcal C_n^{\mathrm{inv}}\).  Pilot selection is independent of the inference subsample.  Conditional on the pilot and outside (1), either the uniform inversion guarantee applies or (2) applies.  In both cases the conditional coverage lower bound is \(1-\alpha-o(1)\).  Taking expectations and using (1) proves the displayed uniform coverage statement.  Exact zeros and ties require no endpoint limit law because they select the inversion branch.

Finally fix a strict regular law \(P_0\).  It lies in the interior of some \(G_J\).  Since \(j_n\to\infty\), the pilot ball shrinks inside the appropriate regular cell and regular selection has probability tending to one.  The inference-subsample numerical intervals differ from their inference-subsample analytic-Jacobian oracle intervals by \(o_{P_0}(N_n^{-1/2})\), by \texttt{thm:pointwise-regular-cell-oracle-recovery}.  Moreover \(m_n=o(n)\), \(N_n/n\to1\), and independence gives
\[
 \bar h_n^{\mathrm i}-\bar h_n
 =\frac{m_n}{n}(\bar h_n^{\mathrm i}-\bar h_n^{\mathrm p})
 =O_{P_0}(\sqrt{m_n}/n)=o_{P_0}(n^{-1/2}).
\]
Continuous differentiability of \(\psi_q\) and covariance consistency transfer this relation to the analytic endpoint centers and standard errors; also
\(N_n^{-1/2}-n^{-1/2}=o(n^{-1/2})\).  Therefore the two outer support endpoints of the split-sample regular slab differ from the corresponding full-sample oracle endpoints by \(o_{P_0}(n^{-1/2})\).  This proves pointwise oracle recovery together with uniform singularity-robust coverage.
